content_html:
DMC's printed shade card reproduces colors on paper and is useful for locating codes and planning color families. DMC also sells a card with small real-thread swatches, which removes some uncertainty introduced by ink, paper and screens.

This guide resolves the situation with practical criteria and avoids automatic fixes that can make the project worse or add unnecessary work.

The difference that matters

Material and construction

On its European site, DMC states that the current printed card lists 500 solid Mouliné Spécial colors plus additional thread ranges. It remains a useful organization tool even when a color-critical match is not required.

Color, sheen and coverage

For choosing between two very close shades, the real-thread card is more reliable because sheen, texture and physical color can be viewed under the same light used for the actual skeins.

When substitution makes sense

The printed card is less costly and convenient for everyday reference. It can be enough for checking numbers, building an approximate palette or locating a color family quickly.

When mixing is risky

For commercial pattern design, a real-thread card is particularly helpful with skin tones, gradients and substitutions. A stitched sample remains the final check because fabric changes how colors are perceived.

How a pattern should state it

Do not treat screenshots of an online chart as a physical color reference. Displays, profiles and image compression prevent any guarantee that the shown shade matches the thread a customer will receive.

Overall, the best solution preserves stability, readability and a reasonable stitching experience. Our editorial content should explain why, and our patterns should apply the same judgment to materials, layout and working notes.

A printed color chart is convenient for organizing numbers and seeing the general structure of the range, but ink on paper cannot reproduce the exact optical behavior of embroidery floss. Thread reflects light, has texture and changes slightly as the strands twist. A real-thread card uses actual fiber samples, making it far more useful when two adjacent shades must be compared precisely.

Digital screens add another layer of uncertainty because brightness, color profile and device calibration vary. A color that appears cool gray on one monitor may look warmer on another. Online swatches are excellent for searching and planning a shortlist, but they should not be the final authority for a portrait palette, brand conversion or replacement inside a partially stitched area.

A real-thread card is especially valuable for choosing transitions. Place the candidate shades beside each other and view them under neutral light, then arrange them from light to dark. The important question is not whether each thread individually resembles a pixel on screen, but whether the group forms the progression the design needs.

Printed cards still have practical advantages: they cost less, are easier to annotate and can be carried without worrying about damaging real samples. They are often sufficient for inventory checks or identifying the approximate family of a missing skein. The best tool depends on whether the task is administrative or color-critical.

For our design workflow, physical thread references should be used when subtle palette decisions affect the product. The PDF can display digital color swatches for orientation, but DMC numbers are the reproducible instruction. Customers should understand that the rendered preview approximates thread color and that the stitched sample is the stronger visual reference.

A real-thread card also helps when choosing fabric. Hold several floss samples directly against the cloth and observe the combination as a group. A thread that looks distinct on white card can lose contrast completely on natural linen or a dyed background.

Keep the card protected from prolonged sunlight and dirt because the samples themselves are references. If a real-thread card becomes faded or stained, it can no longer serve as a reliable comparison standard. Store it closed or away from bright display areas.

For content and customer support, we should distinguish between a digital preview for convenience and a physical reference for color-critical decisions. That language sets realistic expectations and reduces disputes caused by screens displaying thread colors differently.

When comparing two very close samples, fold or bunch the thread so you see a small mass rather than one thin filament. Cross stitch places several reflective strands next to each other, and the perceived color of a stitched block can be easier to judge from a thicker sample.

A physical card is also useful for planning replacements when a palette needs fewer colors. Seeing an entire family together makes it easier to choose which middle shade can disappear while preserving a sensible light-to-dark progression.
